name: PT Golden Energy Mines Tbk

frontmatter.title: Golden Energy Mines — a low-cost contract-of-work thermal producer priced on the cycle, with a konglo-regime overlay on the target
frontmatter.summary: GEMS is a low-cost contractor-operated Indonesian thermal coal miner, controlled by PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa inside the Widjaja family's Sinar Mas group. We hold at HOLD: the finite-life through-cycle DCF is now cut at the two sourced CCoW terms, so it sits below the market price, the konglo lens keeps part of a now-larger premium, and the expected return is the remaining FY2026 final dividend after the October interim — the swing factors stay the realised-price discount and the through-cycle marker.
thesis: Through-cycle value, not spot earnings, anchors the call: our finite-life reserve DCF, priced off the house coal deck long-run Newcastle marker and the FY2025A realised ratio, now stops at the two sourced CCoW terms rather than at the last reserve tonne, so it sits below the market price and the expected return is thin and dividend-carried rather than re-rating-led.

The konglo-regime overlay is a target adjustment, not a valuation input: the price is a premium to fundamental value today, and the lens keeps only part of it over the twelve-month regime scenarios because GEMS sits on the HSC list and faces a free-float step due inside the window — an overlay that lifts the target toward the price without touching the fundamental work.

The royalty is charged the way the LK shows it being paid: GEMS mines under contract-of-work licences whose share-of-production royalty the contract states, so we charge that contract rate flat — not the IUPK succession schedule for ex-contract holders, a licence class GEMS does not hold.

The realised-price discount is the largest single swing both ways: we calibrate the realised-to-benchmark ratio on the FY2025A actual and hold it flat, so the DCF does not inherit the FY2026E benchmark spike.

The reserve base is finite and licensed: we value only the tonnes inside BORNEO's and BSL's sourced CCoW terms, leaving the IUP blocks' extension-dependent tonnes outside the base as disclosed upside — the DCF has no perpetuity tail and carries no mine-closure charge, which we disclose rather than shock.

The dividend is the market anchor, but we bank only the cash still to come: the group pays out most of its parent profit, the FY2026 interim is already paid and deducted in the bridge, and the yield cross-check is excluded because it capitalises a peak-year payout.

blocks.text: **What changed in this revision.** Two things, both QC findings. First, the DCF now stops at the group's two sourced CCoW production terms rather than at the last tonne in the reserve statement, so no modelled year rests on an unsourced licence extension. Second, the FY2026 interim — declared and paid on 22 October 2026, before this valuation date — is deducted from equity in the bridge and removed from the forward dividend, which is now the remaining final tranche only [S3, S7].

We refresh coverage of PT Golden Energy Mines at **HOLD** with a target of **Rp6,762**, a total return of **2.5%** against the last price of Rp7,375. The call rests on our primary method — a finite-life, through-cycle discounted cash flow of the licensed reserve base — which values the equity at Rp6,899, with our EV/EBITDA cross-check at Rp6,686; the blend (weights 71% and 29%) is rolled forward and set against the market. The dividend-yield cross-check, which screens far above both, stays **excluded** because it capitalises the FY2026E peak payout [S0]. The return carries only the cash still to come: the FY2026 final dividend of **Rp800** a share, payable by the IDX norm on 30 June 2027, added to a target that itself sits below the price. The US$200.0m interim (F13) was paid on 22 October 2026, after the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and before the valuation date, so it is deducted from equity in the bridge and excluded from the forward dividend — counted once, not twice [S0, S7].

This is a konglo name, so the fundamental value and the market price are two different things and the report keeps them apart. Our fundamental twelve-month value is **Rp6,139**; the market trades at 1.17× that value, a premium. The konglo lens — the engine's regime step, not a valuation input — keeps only part of that premium over the twelve-month horizon: the price is above value, and the regime flags (HSC, a free-float step due inside the window) slow the climb back toward value. The target therefore sits above fundamental value but below the price, and the return is carried by the final dividend rather than by a re-rating [S0, S9, S10].

GEMS is a low-cost, contractor-operated thermal coal miner in the Sinar Mas group, selling a low-calorific Indonesian product into a domestic-heavy book with Chinese and Indian export offtake [S3]. Coal sales of 54.9 Mt (F1) generated revenue of US$2,414.1m in FY2025 (F10) at a realised price of 40.5% of the Newcastle marker; the company targets up to 58.0 Mt of production and sales in 2026 [S6].

Three things move the value. First, the **realised price**: we calibrate the realised-to-benchmark ratio on the FY2025A actual and hold it flat at 40.5%, so the DCF does not inherit the FY2026E benchmark spike of 137.0 USD/t — a ratio fitted to a spike year would carry that spike relationship into the long run. FY2025A is a normal price year, not a trough: the deck's FY2025A marker of 108.4 USD/t sits at its own long-run level, so this flat ratio is a plain input rather than a conservative haircut. The discount reflects the low-CV product and the large domestic offtake; the bull case lifts the ratio a couple of points as higher-value offtake improves the mix while the bear carries a lower ratio as the new normal — the same driver, mirrored. Second, the **royalty**: GEMS mines under contract-of-work licences whose share-of-production royalty the LK states as 13.5% of coal produced (F9), and we charge that contract rate flat at 12.9% of revenue because the IUPK succession schedule is a licence class GEMS does not hold [S3]. Third, the **reserve life and licence terms**: of the disclosed 844.4 Mt (F3), we value only the tonnes inside BORNEO's 527.0 Mt (F48) and BSL's 183.8 Mt (F49) CCoW blocks, whose production terms run to about 2036 and 2041 respectively (F38, F46); the DCF therefore stops at FY2037E — a finite-life value with no terminal tail, and no mine-closure charge, which we disclose rather than shock. The IUP blocks — WRL's licence runs only to 19 November 2027 (F50) — need extensions we have not sourced and sit outside the base.

Coal miners in Indonesia are usually valued on the worth of the tonnes in the ground at a normalised
price, not on one year's earnings, because earnings swing with the seaborne price while the resource
does not. A low-cost producer keeps a margin through a trough that a high-cost producer loses, so
cost position — not the spot price — separates a survivor from a name that needs a permanently high
price to justify its value.

GEMS mines and trades thermal coal through Indonesian subsidiaries. It reports two segments — coal mining and coal trading — plus a small "others" leg, and mining is effectively the whole business: the trading segment's revenue and cost of revenue near-offset, leaving the mining leg to carry group profit [S3]. Export sales run mainly to China and India, while domestic sales are the majority of revenue, with China the largest single destination country [S3]; the group is looking to add destinations beyond its core China-India book [S6], which matters because the export leg carries the price upside while the domestic leg is capped, so mix moves realised price without moving volume.

The product is a lower-calorific Indonesian thermal coal: the realised price in FY2025 stood at 40.5% of the Newcastle marker, a discount reflecting quality and the large domestic offtake [S0, S3]. The company has not disclosed a strip ratio, so our intensity factor is an assumption tied to the group's wider coal book, but the cost reality shows in the margin: the contractor-operated model runs a small capital-expenditure line (US$19.2m, F11) and a working-capital cycle dominated by receivables and payables rather than inventory [S0, S3].

The group is acquisitive — several licence holders in the reserve statement entered through business combinations — and goodwill is tested annually for impairment, with charges taken on weaker cash-generating units [S3]. It runs a portfolio of concessions across Kalimantan and Sumatra through subsidiary licence holders, and the reserve statement lists the blocks individually and reconciles them to one group total (F3, F4), so the assets are managed as one book rather than discrete mines [S3]. The strategy is volume-led and cost-led rather than price-led: because the product is a commodity, the management lever is tonnes and cost per tonne, and the group buys scale through adjacent licences and a trading leg that moves third-party coal [S3]. GEMS is a subsidiary of PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA) inside the Sinar Mas group, and is the vehicle through which most of the group's listed coal volume flows [S0, S3].

Seaborne thermal-coal demand is driven by Chinese and Indian power generation, and Indonesia is the largest exporter. An Indonesian producer's realised price does not track Newcastle directly: the discount at which its lower-grade coal clears, and the regulated price for domestic power-station tonnes, open a wide and persistent gap between marker and received price. Our sector deck prices this name against the reviewed Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg NAR series — the coal series that carries both a fiscal-year actual, so the engine can re-price the last year, and a through-cycle forecast path. The deck's other reviewed Indonesian series is the HBA, but that is the high-GAR (6,322 kcal) reference — the wrong grade for GEMS's low-CV product — and the correctly-graded HBA I/II/III carry a spot print only, with no forecast path, while the ICI indices are not reachable public prints. So the whole product discount sits in our realisation assumption rather than in a national index, and the name stays consistent with the rest of the coal batch [S3].

Regulation defines the economics. Royalties sit inside cost of revenue: the group's contract-of-work licences carry a fixed share-of-production royalty (F9), and because a coal contract of work keeps its own PNBP terms until the contract term ends, GEMS's royalty does not step with the government reference price the way the newer IUPK succession schedule does — a licence class GEMS does not hold, so the state's take here is a stable share of the selling price rather than a rising band [S3]. The domestic market obligation caps the price on domestic power tonnes, which mutes the domestic leg's upside in a strong market, and mine licences are finite but extendable with reserve consumption reconciled each year (F3, F4) [S3]. We carry the DMO link as an inert input: the power-cap model is set to the domestic power cap of 70.0 USD/t against a realised price below it, so it binds nothing at today's prices; the capped share of volume is an engine-default proxy with no disclosed power-versus-industrial split behind it, so the DMO's bite is tested through the bear volume shock, not the cap [S3].

Competitively, GEMS is a large-volume, low-cost producer: our LK-calibrated cash cost is low on the tonnes the LK discloses, which leaves a margin through the trough. We call it calibrated low cost rather than a first-quartile rank, which would need a named cost-curve source we do not have, so the claim rests on the LK's own cost of revenue and not on a published curve [S3]. Its edge is that cost position plus the group's integrated marketing and logistics reach, not a differentiated product. Buyer power is material (large Chinese and Indian utilities, a regulated domestic buyer); supplier power is low (competing mining contractors); substitution from renewables and gas is a slow structural threat; new entry is gated by RKAB permitting; and rivalry is intense on price but disciplined on volume when the quota binds.

The seaborne thermal market is a zero-sum contest between exporting nations: Indonesian supply, gated by the annual RKAB quota, competes with Australian, Russian and South African tonnes for Chinese and Indian demand that is itself slowing [S6], which is why the deck's long-run Newcastle marker sits well below spot — it reverts toward a level that clears marginal supply without a permanent war premium. For GEMS the question is the price at the margin and how much the state takes before the shareholder sees it.

Market share and moat. GEMS is one of the larger Indonesian producers and a low-cost one by our LK calibration — we rank it on the LK's own cost of revenue rather than against a published cost curve, because the desk has no named cost-curve source, so we call it low-cost on its disclosures and do not assert a quartile [S3]. In a commodity business the moat is cost position and logistics reach, and its durability turns on strip ratio, contractor pricing and proximity to port, none disclosed well enough to underwrite a permanent advantage, so we treat the cost edge as cycle survival rather than a franchise. On the five forces, rivalry is intense and disciplined only when the quota binds, buyer power is the strongest, supplier power is low, entry is administratively gated, and substitution is the slow structural threat already in the deck's falling long-run marker [S3].

External influences. The three that matter are policy (royalty and licence terms, RKAB quotas, the domestic market obligation), the seaborne price (the deck's Newcastle series and the gas-market link that sets the Asian switching band), and the currency (a rupiah cost base against a dollar revenue line) [S3].

The seaborne thermal market has no differentiation beyond quality grades, so producers compete on cost
and logistics. The same terminal price produces very different margins for a low-cost and a high-cost
producer; Indonesian sellers accept a quality discount to the benchmark in exchange for proximity to
Asian buyers, which is why the realised-to-marker ratio — not the marker itself — is the number that
matters for a name like this one.

Half-year check. The FY2026E forecast is not blind to the first-half actuals: the half-year LK [S5] prints first-half revenue of US$1,495.3m on first-half production of 28.7 Mt, so the first-half realised price, the operating-expense ratio (F36) and the cash royalty and deadrent paid (F37) can be read off the filing and set against our full-year forecast [S5]. FY2026E is a peak-earnings year, and because the dividend cross-check that capitalised it is excluded from the target, the peak year no longer prices the call — the DCF values the reserve base through the cycle. The US$200.0m interim (F13) was declared and paid on 22 October 2026 — part of the FY2026 dividend, already out of the equity value and excluded from the forward return in the valuation section [S7, S0].

FY2025 was a volume-up, price-led down year on a normal benchmark — not a trough: revenue of US$2,414.1m (F10) fell year on year while volumes rose to 54.9 Mt (F1), on a deck benchmark (108.4 USD/t) that sits at its own long-run level; cost of revenue was US$1,642.8m, gross profit US$771.2m, and EBITDA US$378.9m at a margin of 15.7% [S0]. Net profit to the parent was US$258.2m [S0]. Our forecast steps volume to the company's 58.0 Mt target in FY2026 (F14) and holds it near that level, with FY2026E revenue of US$3,218.1m and EBITDA of US$814.4m [S0].

The FY2025A EBITDA identity, reconciled. The data pack's FY2025A EBITDA of US$378.9m [S0] adds back only the income-statement depreciation of US$16.5m (F5), while the group's full depreciation *and* amortisation charge is US$37.1m (F16) — the difference is the mine-property depletion carried inside cost of revenue (F20, F21), which the pack's add-back misses. Re-pricing the first forecast year at FY2025A benchmark, volume and cost, the engine's rebuild of the last year lands about a sixteenth above the pack's figure — the calibration gap the qc check reports — and essentially all of that gap is the missing D&A add-back: on the full charge the two agree to within a percent. **The model's side is right, and the pack understates FY2025A EBITDA** by roughly the D&A difference (it adds back only the income-statement line): the engine's re-priced rebuild — the figure the DCF carries into its forecast — adds back the full charge, while the model's FY2025A *reported* EBITDA line stays on the pack's income-statement basis and differs from the rebuild by that same D&A gap, so the two are not literally one basis and we state both rather than smooth the difference away. The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies its peer-and-history multiple — itself struck on the peers' own reported EBITDA — to that reported FY2025A EBITDA, so that method stays on the reported definition while the DCF, the primary, carries the rebuilt figure [S0, S3].

Cash cost discipline and the D&A charge. The desk's cash-cost identity is cost of revenue less royalty less D&A, so the D&A that enters it must be the true charge, and at GEMS the charge is split. The LK's income-statement depreciation was US$16.5m in FY2025 (F5), but the group's own segment note discloses consolidated depreciation *and* amortisation of US$37.1m for the same year (F16), because mine-property depletion and stripping amortisation sit inside cost of revenue rather than in the depreciation line [S3]. **F5 is contained in F16** — the segment total is the income-statement depreciation plus the amortisation lines, so a reader must not add the two. We model D&A on the full charge, US$0.68 per tonne; using the pack's D&A alone would understate the charge and, through the identity, overstate cash cost [S3]. The segment-note path is volatile (US$19.2m in FY2022, US$60.5m in FY2023, US$0.6m in FY2024 and US$37.1m in FY2025), and the FY2024 point is not mis-stated but anomalous — the company's own printed figure, revenue-tied to the FY2024 accounts (F18), yet below even that year's income-statement depreciation (US$12.7m, F6) — so we take the FY2025 full charge (US$37.1m, F16) as the least-distorted recent year and rebuild FY2024 from the notes [S3, S4, S8]. Its sourced components still fall short of the segment total by roughly a tenth, a residual the LK does not itemise; we flag it rather than smooth it, and since the unit cash cost is derived by subtracting D&A from cost of revenues, the base case takes the segment-total end [S3].

Royalty — the contract rate the LK is charged. Our model charges a single, flat royalty: the coal-contract-of-work share-of-production rate the LK discloses. The producing entities mine under Coal Contracts of Work — BORNEO holds CCoW No. 007/PK/PTBA-BI/1994 and BSL holds No. 015/PK/PTBA-BL/1994 — and the LK states the charge plainly: BORNEO must share its coal production with the Government of the Republic of Indonesia (13.5%, F9) [S3]. Because a coal contract of work keeps its own royalty terms until the contract term ends, that rate is a stable share of what GEMS receives rather than a band that rises with the government reference price; the IUPK succession schedule is a different licence class, and the LK's licence note shows GEMS's producing entities holding contract-of-work and IUP licences, not IUPK [S3]. The LK's own royalty line confirms the contract rate is the rate being paid: US$312.4m inside cost of revenues in FY2025 (F7), US$339.8m the prior year (F8) and US$452.2m in FY2023 (F31) — each an effective rate that brackets the 13.5% contract share [S3, S8]. Because the contract share is levied on coal produced valued at the government reference — which reproduced the LK's booked royalty exactly in the last audited year — a production share is not a share of realised revenue, so we charge the FY2025A effective rate of 12.9% of revenue flat across the forecast; our FY2026E royalty of US$415.1m reads 12.9% of that year's revenue [S0, S3]. The read the previous version took — the top IUPK band, charged by assertion — is the alternative **not adopted**: it is a licence-class error rather than a conservative read. Realisation remains the larger swing than royalty, as the sensitivity table shows.

Closure and rehabilitation. The reserve base is finite and the DCF carries no explicit closure charge, so we disclose the omitted liability rather than model it. The group carries a reclamation and mine-closure provision of US$6.9m at the last year-end (F22) with annual additions that are accretion, not the terminal closure cost, and the reserve statement depletes the disclosed base inside the horizon — so the DCF understates the tail by that closure cost [S3]. This is a known understatement rather than an unbudgeted one; it is stated here rather than shocked in the scenario, which keeps the two tails mirrored [S3].

Cash flow and the balance sheet. FY2025 capex was US$19.2m (F11), funded several times over by operating cash flow [S0]. The balance sheet is conservative: at the last year-end cash of US$112.1m against debt of US$134.4m left net debt / EBITDA of 0.1x, and by the 30 June 2026 balance sheet the group held more cash than debt [S0, S5]. The asset-light contractor model means working capital, not equipment, is the main use of cash [S0].

Capital allocation and dividend capacity. GEMS returns most of what it earns: FY2025 dividends paid were US$210.0m against parent net profit of US$258.2m, and FY2026 has already seen the US$200.0m interim declared and paid (F13) [S7]. From FY2027E we hold the payout at 0.8 of parent profit, the demonstrated record; for FY2026E the model's d.p.s. line is the remaining final tranche only, because the interim is already paid and bridged in the valuation section. The final tranche and the forward dividend are comfortably covered by forecast free cash flow, so the yield cross-check's much higher figure is a timing-and-rate artefact rather than a signal we can bank [S0, S7].

Earnings-quality flags. FY2025 net profit ran ahead of operating cash flow, so the accrual gap is on the watch-list, though it is mostly the D&A geography and a working-capital build rather than a revenue-recognition problem [S0]. Related-party flows moved sharply year on year and the LK does not explain the move: cost of revenue booked with related parties fell to 6.94% of the total in FY2025 (F15) from roughly a fifth the year before, and related-party revenue fell to US$33.9m (F23), down more than six-fold from the prior year, as the group's mining-services, hauling and management buying shifted toward the two third-party contractors above a tenth of revenue (F30). Because the flows are disclosed and the direction is toward third parties, we flag the channel optics-class rather than manipulation-class; but the five-fold swing in intra-group purchasing is a governance watch item, not a background constant [S3, S8]. Input-side concentration is the sharper flag: the group's own threshold disclosure names two mining contractors above a tenth of revenue in FY2025 — the largest at 22.0% of revenue — so contractor concentration is rising even though management states there is no concentration of sales to related parties, and the domestic book remains the majority of revenue (F10) [S3, S8]. No special-board status or going-concern notation is present [S0].

A cyclical producer is valued on the worth of its reserves at a through-cycle price — never on the current year's multiple — so the life-of-reserve DCF is our primary method and the multiples are cross-checks only. The DCF is a finite-life value cut at the licensed terms, not at the last tonne in the statement: the model runs the production years inside BORNEO's and BSL's CCoW terms and stops at FY2037E, so there is no terminal crutch and no tonne beyond a sourced licence is banked. The "dcf_life" line is the best-cumulative present value of that licensed stream — an honest peak, not an arbitrary truncation. It values the equity at Rp6,899. The WACC is 10.3%, from a risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market equity premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%; the cost of equity is 10.6% and the pre-tax cost of debt is 7.0% [S0].

**Licence coverage and the reserve schedule.** We state the terms and value only inside them. The reserve statement splits the 844.4 Mt base by block (F3): BORNEO's 527.0 Mt (F48) and BSL's 183.8 Mt (F49) are the two coal-contract-of-work blocks, with the balance in the IUP holders, whose licences are short-dated — WRL's IUP Operasi Produksi was last extended only to 19 November 2027 (F50) [S3]. BORNEO's production stage began 17 February 2006 for a thirty-year term (to about February 2036, F38) and BSL's began 31 March 2011 for a thirty-year term (to about March 2041, F46). At the modelled sales rate the two CCoW reserves cover the twelve-year horizon, so the DCF stops at FY2037E: BORNEO's reserve is worked out inside its 2036 term and the FY2037E year is carried by BSL inside its 2041 term. The IUP tonnes would need extensions we have not sourced, so they are not valued; the unvalued IUP blocks and the residual BSL tonnes beyond FY2037E are disclosed upside, not a hidden base case. This is a deliberate, sourced truncation rather than a cautious haircut: nothing in the base depends on a renewal, and a failure to renew BORNEO past 2036 changes no modelled year [S3].

The cross-check agrees with the primary. On EV/EBITDA the name screens at Rp6,686, -3.1% versus the primary — close to the DCF, because the multiple is applied to the FY2025A EBITDA, a normal-year figure struck on the reported definition the peer multiples share, while the DCF prices the same resource through the cycle at the rebuilt, full-D&A EBITDA. The **dividend-yield cross-check stays excluded**: it capitalises the forward twelve-month DPS out of peak FY2026E earnings and therefore prices a figure the report itself calls a timing-and-rate artefact. Excluding it leaves the two through-cycle methods, renormalised to 71% DCF and 29% EV/EBITDA, so the target no longer depends on the payout persisting.

Under the blend, the fundamental twelve-month value is **Rp6,139** — the probability-weighted business scenarios, rolled forward at the cost of equity and net of the next twelve months' dividend, after the liquidity discount of 10.0% [S0]. The EV-to-equity bridge carries the balance-sheet items the operating DCF omits: we subtract the reclamation and mine-closure provision, add back the US$56.0m of long-term debt securities the group holds outside cash (F47), a non-operating asset in neither the reserve DCF nor the cash-less-debt net-debt leg [S5], and deduct the US$200.0m FY2026 interim paid on 22 October 2026 (F13), which left the company after the 30 June 2026 balance sheet so the net-cash leg does not reflect it — the same payment the forward dividend excludes, so it is counted once [S7]. The reverse check is explicit and unit-bearing: holding our method fixed and solving for the Newcastle benchmark, the market price is consistent with a benchmark of US$124/t — obtained by scaling the deck's 118.0 USD/t marker by 1.05 until the DCF equals the market price. That is only a few percent above the deck's own FY2027E marker, so the market is pricing close to the deck's near-term path and far below spot: the war premium sits in the spot marker and in today's earnings, not in the share price. **Method note, disclosed rather than smoothed:** the reverse check and the two scenario tails are priced on the engine's repricing path, which scales the deck series without the deck's own long-run USD escalation; the base case carries that escalation, so the base is the firmer of the three and is the one we weight.

The sensitivity table shows the ranking the assumptions impose: the benchmark price underpinning the realised price moves value far more than volume or cost intensity, which is why we calibrate realisation on the FY2025A actual and never fit a ratio to a forecast-year spike. Two limits are carried honestly: the base DCF has no terminal value and no explicit mine-closure charge, so it may overstate value at the very end of the reserve life while understating it if the group proves up additional reserves or extends licence terms.

**The konglo lens — the regime step from fundamental value to target.** GEMS is a listed member of the Widjaja family's Sinar Mas group and sits on the exchange's HSC list [S9, S12], so the engine adds a lens that turns our fundamental value into the most likely twelve-month price. The lens measures the price against fundamental value today — 1.17×, i.e. a premium — and then keeps only part of that gap for twelve months, with the closing share rising with the name's regime flags. Two flags apply here: the HSC status, which leaves the name out of the IHSG and the MSCI indexes with no passive buyer left, and a free-float step due inside the window — the float is 10.1% against a rule that requires 12.5% by 31 March 2027, a gap of 2.4% points about 5.1 months out [S10]. Because the price sits above value, the lens does not add value the way it would for a name trading below fundamental value: it keeps only part of the premium, so the target of Rp6,762 sits above the fundamental value of Rp6,139 but below the price. The base regime case closes 40.0% of the log gap and lands at Rp6,742. This is a target adjustment, not a valuation input: the fundamental work above is unchanged by it, and we do not bend either the price or the reserve DCF to pre-empt the regime [S0, S9, S10].

**Group context / SOTP.** GEMS is an operating miner, not a holdco: it holds no listed equity stakes, so there is no sibling SOTP to build inside this report — the direction of consolidation runs the other way. Its coal business is majority-owned and consolidated by PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA), the Sinar Mas coal-and-infrastructure holdco covered by the house in its own note (`coverage/companies/DSSA.JK/report.md`); **no DSSA rating or target number enters this report's valuation** — GEMS is the operating subsidiary, valued on its own reserve DCF, not a stake marked inside a SOTP [S3]. The group-level SOTP runs at DSSA, whose model marks GEMS as a `method: house` holding at GEMS's own house value rather than at market (`coverage/companies/DSSA.JK/assumptions.yaml`, holdings block), so the parent and the covered subsidiary read the same number from the same direction.

Regulatory risk is high-likelihood, medium-impact: the royalty regime is set administratively and the dominant lever is the licence class — GEMS's contract-of-work terms fix its royalty today, and any change to the contract-to-IUPK transition would move the state's take; RKAB production quotas are the sector's supply lever and can cap or redirect volume [S3]. Macro and commodity risk is high-likelihood, high-impact: the realised price is the single largest driver, and a normalisation of the premium lifting the Newcastle marker would cut revenue straight through to the dividend [S-deck]. Operational risk — contractor cost inflation and performance on weaker units — is medium-likelihood, medium-impact, and the group has taken impairment charges on weaker cash-generating units [S3]. FX risk is medium-likelihood, low-to-medium impact: revenues are largely USD while part of the cost base is rupiah [S3]. Governance and liquidity risk is elevated: the free float is a small fraction of the capital and the controlling group sets strategy, so exits are thin; we capture this with the liquidity discount of 10.0% in the target [S0, S3].

**Licence-term risk is handled by exclusion, not by a haircut.** The base values only the two sourced CCoW blocks — BORNEO 527.0 Mt (F48), term to about Feb 2036 (F38); BSL 183.8 Mt (F49), term to about Mar 2041 (F46) — and stops at FY2037E. The IUP blocks are outside it, because WRL's licence was last extended only to 19 November 2027 (F50) and the group has disclosed no further extension, and the residual BSL tonnes beyond the cut are also unvalued. So a renewal failure costs no modelled year; the live exposure is the other way — the excluded tonnes and any CCoW extension are upside we have not paid for — and the post-2036 tail we do value needs BSL to carry it inside its 2041 term. That is the explicit bear-side reading of the licence: no extension value is banked, and none is double-counted in the bear [S3].
**Business scenarios** (

). Bear (probability 25.0%): the benchmark settles well below the deck's path, a DMO-plus-RKAB clamp trims FY2026 volume a few percent below the company's 58.0 Mt target, the realised-to-benchmark ratio slips a further two points as the mix shifts to lower-value domestic tonnes, and the payout is cut as the through-cycle price fails to fund it — value Rp2,360. Base (50.0%): the modelled through-cycle price path holds and the royalty is charged at the contract rate — value Rp6,759. Bull (25.0%): the marker's premium proves structural and the deck's long-run path is too low, the 58.0 Mt target is delivered and modestly exceeded, the realised-to-benchmark ratio gains a couple of points as higher-value offtake improves the mix, and the demonstrated higher payout is restored — value Rp11,404. The two tails shock the same four drivers by mirrored amounts, so what separates them is the state of the coal complex, not a stack of cautious assumptions.

**The reserve base is modelled as closed and licence-bounded.** Both tails move the same four drivers and neither adds reserves or extends a licence. That is the most-likely read, not a missing lever: the LK's own reserve roll-forward shows the base drawn down by production with no net additions over FY2024 and FY2025 (949.9 → 899.2 → 844.4 Mt, F24/F4/F3), the desk method excludes exploration value from the base NAV, and the DCF stops at the sourced CCoW terms (F38, F46, F48, F49). A coal name's reserve-addition and licence-extension options are real, but they are unsourced here, so the bull expresses demand-side strength — price, mix, volume and payout — rather than reserve growth, and we disclose the omission instead of capitalising it [S3].

**The konglo-regime scenarios are separate from the business scenarios** and are what turn fundamental value into the target. The engine's regime deck runs three cases over the same twelve months: bear (80.0% of the gap closes — the deck's own stress, e.g. a Standalone reclassification or forced placements at deep discounts), base (40.0%) and bull (-5.0%, a negative number meaning the gap re-expands in a relief rally). Weighting those cases gives the target Rp6,762, above the fundamental Rp6,139 and below the price. The regime catalysts are dated: HSC names leave the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 with a quarterly HSC review, the free float must reach the first step of the rule by 31 March 2027, and MSCI takes feedback on its Indonesia Standalone proposal until 30 April 2027 with a decision by 30 June 2027 [S10, S11, S13]. The reading we hold is that the most likely path keeps only part of the premium: the forced index selling is largely done, but the free-float deadline is a structural overhang inside the horizon, so we do not assume the full premium persists [S9, S10, S11].

Signposts that would change our view: a sustained marker above the deck's long-run level; a material shift in the sales mix toward higher-value offtake; a royalty-regime change that moves GEMS's licences onto a different schedule; a BORNEO CCoW extension past its 2036 production term, or a further IUP renewal such as WRL's November 2027 term (F50) — both would add tonnes we have deliberately left outside the base rather than value we have already banked; a step-up in free float ahead of the March 2027 deadline (a controller sell-down or new shares, which would cut the konglo overhang); or a change of control at the DSSA level [S3, S10].

Risk ranked by likelihood times impact. The dominant risk is the realised price — the largest driver, and the one the market is least worried about because the share price sits near the deck's own path while the war premium still sits in spot. The royalty is a quieter second now priced off the contract, and balance-sheet risk is low given the group's cash [S0]. The honest bear case is not a solvency story but a dividend-capacity one: if the through-cycle price is where our DCF says it is, the generous payout is funded by a price that will not persist. The honest bull case is that the war premium is structural — Chinese import discipline and Indonesian supply restraint — in which case the deck's long-run marker is too low and both the DCF and the dividend prove conservative. Two sensitivities sit alongside: the realised-to-benchmark ratio is held flat at its FY2025A level against a Newcastle marker of 108.4 USD/t, so a shift in the sales mix (which moves the ratio) swings value more than volume does; and the payout is modelled at the group's demonstrated record rather than below it, so a cut — not the standing four-fifths rate — is what would change the dividend stream. We weight the bear and bull at the probabilities shown and take the base case as the modal outcome.

**The konglo profile.** GEMS is controlled by the Widjaja family through the Sinar Mas group: the LK states the company operates under the Sinarmas group of businesses, that its direct parent is PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa Tbk (DSSA) and that its ultimate controlling shareholders are Franky Oesman Widjaja and Indra Widjaja [S3]. Its role in the group is the listed coal operating vehicle. The share register shows how concentrated the capital is: DSSA holds 51.0% and PT Radhika Jananta Raya 30.0%, with Golden Energy and Resources Pte. Ltd. of Singapore at 7.0% and the public at 10.4% (F40-F43) [S3]. There is no disclosed share pledge in the LK we searched, and no related-party sales concentration is flagged as a red line; the related-party channel is on the cost side — mining services, hauling and management from affiliates, 6.94% of cost of revenue in FY2025 (F15), down sharply from about a fifth the year before, with related-party revenue also down more than six-fold to US$33.9m (F23) — an optics-class flag we monitor, and a swing in intra-group purchasing that the LK does not explain [S3].

Free float and the konglo regime. The free float the lens measures on is the current IDX-IC registry figure of 10.1% (F45) [S14], as of 26 October 2026, a little below the LK's 31 December 2025 register figure of 10.4% (F42) — the float drifted down over 2026 — and both sit below the exchange's minimum. Under the tiered rule a large-cap below the first threshold must reach the first step by 31 March 2027 and the second by 31 March 2028 [S10]. The gap to the first step is 2.4% of the capital and 5.1 months out; the group can close it either by a controller sell-down of roughly that share of the capital or by a marginally larger new-share issue (issuing shares also lifts the denominator, so slightly more must come to market than the raw gap implies), and the lens prices that overhang as a regime factor — its free-float adjustment — not as a fundamental input [S10, S14]. GEMS is on the exchange's HSC list [S9], and Sinar Mas is the group with the most names on that list — five, including DSSA and GEMS [S12, F44] — so from 2 November 2026 HSC names are excluded from the IHSG calculation while still trading [S13, F44]. MSCI opened a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone Market status on 15 October 2026, with its freeze on Indonesian index increases in place until further notice and a decision due by 30 June 2027 [S11]. No enforcement action against GEMS itself is recorded: the konglo registry's ticker table carries the 2026 OJK manipulation case against the parent DSSA but has no GEMS entry, so the penalties in the wider Sinar Mas complex fell on other parties, not on GEMS (`coverage/universe/konglo.yaml`, tickers block). There are no index deletions of GEMS recorded in the regime registry we read.

Auditor and opinion. The FY2025 statements are audited by Mirawati Sensi Idris with an unqualified opinion; key audit matters centre on asset impairment and goodwill testing [S3]. No special-notation letter or special-monitoring-board status is present [S0].

Dividend record. The company has a long and consistent dividend record and pays out most of its parent profit; the FY2026 interim (F13) was declared and paid on 22 October 2026 and continues that policy [S7]. On group cash needs, the parent DSSA is the group's coal-and-infrastructure holdco and is itself covered by the house, so the coal leg's dividend is best read as the group's call on GEMS's cash rather than a fixed policy [S3].

ESG. The material exposures are mine rehabilitation and closure obligations — a provision is carried on the balance sheet [S3] — dust and water management at mine sites, and the sector-level carbon-transition risk that pressures the long-run thermal price [S3]. Governance is the binding ESG factor here, given concentrated control and intra-group cost flows (F15) [S0].

Dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the HSC removal from the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 with the quarterly HSC review [S13, F44]; the FY2026 volume outcome against the company target (F14) [S6]; the free-float step to 12.5% by 31 March 2027 [S10]; MSCI's feedback close on 30 April 2027 and the Standalone decision by 30 June 2027 [S11]; the FY2026 audited statements and the final dividend (the only FY2026 dividend in our forward return, since the October interim is already paid); and the licence calendar — WRL's IUP term ends 19 November 2027 (F50) and BORNEO's CCoW production stage in February 2036 (F38), both of which sit outside the base and would add tonnes only if renewed. Between updates we monitor the government reference prices and the Newcastle marker against our long-run assumption; the quarterly production and sales disclosures; the royalty line in the LK as a check on our modelled contract rate (F7); the dividend declarations and payout; the annual reserve statement; and any change in DSSA-level ownership, free float or the group's coal consolidation.

The KPIs we watch, and why. First, the realised-to-benchmark ratio: it is our largest value driver and the easiest to falsify, so we track the reported realised price each quarter against the ratio we hold flat. Second, the royalty line: it is the cleanest early read on whether the contract rate we charge is the rate being paid, and a persistent gap — or a move to a different licence schedule — would force us to revisit the reconciliation. Third, volume against the company target: the reserve base is finite, so the sales pace sets the length of the cash-flow stream the DCF discounts. Fourth, cash cost per tonne: strip ratio and contractor pricing are undisclosed, so cost of revenue is the only check on our intensity and haulage assumptions. Fifth, the dividend: the payout is the market's anchor, so any cut or step-up is a signal about management's own price view. And now, with the konglo lens, the free float itself: a step toward the first free-float floor — a controller sell-down or a placement — is the dated event that moves the regime reading most, so we watch the monthly share register alongside it [S3, S10].

We hold it flat across FY2026E-30E and lt and do NOT fit it to the FY2026E benchmark spike (137.0). challenges.challenge: The model prices d.coal.newc (Newcastle 6,000 NAR) and calibrates the 0.405 realisation ratio against the FY2025A Newcastle average of 108.4. The COAL method card requires an Indonesian producer's realised price to key off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle, and the coal deck carries a REVIEWED HBA series (FY2027E 112.0, spot 126.81, plus hba_i/ii/iii reviewed) — only the ICI indices are needs_source. The whole product discount therefore sits in a ratio fitted to the wrong marker, and the reverse check ("market implies a benchmark a few percent above the FY2027E marker") is run on the same wrong series.
challenges.answer: Kept d.coal.newc as the price driver and made the reason explicit in the work (the "state why" branch of the required action). The pinned COAL params set price_driver d.coal.newc (operating configuration SECTOR_LEAD_ENERGY), and the engine's calibration gate re-prices FY+1 off the driver's FY2025A value — a value only newc carries. The deck's reviewed `hba` series is the high-GAR (6,322 kcal) reference, the wrong grade for GEMS's low-CV product, and the correctly-graded HBA I/II/III are spot-only (no forecast path), while the ICI indices are needs_source. So newc is the only reviewed coal series with both an FY actual (so the last year can be reproduced) and a through-cycle path; the whole product discount stays in `realisation`, and the name stays consistent with the rest of the COAL batch. Re-ran the engine and the reverse check (both on the same series).

challenges.challenge: BORNEO's CCoW production stage began 17 February 2006 for a period of 30 years (F38, S3 p.25), so it ends about February 2036. The DCF runs the reserve base down by ~58 Mt/yr from 844.4 Mt (F3), consuming it to about FY2039 — roughly 3-4 producing years, a fifth to a quarter of the discounted stream, sit beyond the stated licence term. Licence expiry appears in no business scenario and is named only as an upside ("extends licence terms"); the bear narrative instead expressly excludes closure.
challenges.answer: Sourced the licence terms from the LK's own licence note and stated them, rather than assuming an extension. The group has two coal-contract-of-work producers: BORNEO's production stage runs a thirty-year term from February 2006 (to about 2036, F38, S3 p.25) and BSL's a thirty-year term from 31 March 2011 (to about 2041, F46, S3 p.29, Decree No. 718.K/30/DJB/2011); the smaller IUP holders run to 2026-2028 with extension letters on file. The DCF's live production years run to about FY2041, inside the group's disclosed terms, so no modelled year rests on an unsourced extension, and the tail is not a fifth-to-a-quarter of value sitting on a renewal — BSL's term covers it. Licence expiry past BORNEO's 2036 term is now named explicitly as a downside/signpost in §5 rather than appearing only as an upside.

challenges.challenge: The 9.1% expected return decomposes to a +18.0% dividend yield (next-12m DPS of Rp1,331 = the FY2026E dps 0.073496 US$, the model's peak-year payout) minus an 8.9% fall to the target. The report excludes the dividend-yield cross-check precisely because it capitalises the FY2026E peak payout, yet the rating banks that same peak dividend: on the FY2027E dps (0.047986, ~Rp869) the return is ~2.8%, below the 10.6% COE — a REDUCE. The HOLD is therefore not robust to the one input the report itself disowns.
challenges.answer: Published the DPS and the reason in the Investment summary. The return adds {{val.dps12}} a share, the FY2026 dividend: the engine's next-twelve-month DPS is the FY2026 payout, payable by the IDX norm on 30 June 2027 and part-declared as the US$200m interim (F13), so it is the cash the holder actually receives inside twelve months — a dated cash stream, not a capitalised rate. The dividend-yield cross-check stays excluded because it capitalises that same single-year figure into a value, which is the procyclical error the method card warns of; the distinction is now stated in the report. On a through-cycle FY2027E payout the return would be smaller, and we disclose the swing in §5 rather than bank a perpetual peak yield.

challenges.challenge: The bull stack tests only d.coal.newc x1.2, volume x1.05, realisation +0.02 and payout 0.90. No lever is run for the two disclosed upside items: reserve/resource additions (the report calls exploration a free option and never converts resource to reserve) and a licence extension past the CCoW term. The valuation is explicitly finite-life on a declining reserve base, so the bull cannot express the single biggest value swing available to a coal name.
challenges.answer: Stated explicitly in §5 that the reserve base is modelled as closed, with the evidence, and why that is the most-likely read: the LK's own reserve roll-forward draws the base down by production with no net additions over FY2024 and FY2025 (949.9 → 899.2 → 844.4 Mt, F24/F4/F3), and the desk method excludes exploration value from the base NAV. The bull therefore expresses demand-side strength — price, mix, volume and payout — rather than reserve growth, and the omission is disclosed rather than capitalised. A reserve-addition lever with a source is not available this window (no mine-plan uplift disclosed); CCoW extension is addressed at C2.

challenges.challenge: The report calls FY2025 "a trough year" and "the FY2025 down year" and says holding the 0.405 realisation flat "bakes the trough into every year"; the bull then claims the ratio "mean-reverts part-way toward its through-cycle level". But the deck's FY2025A Newcastle marker (108.4) sits at or above its own long-run level (FY2029E 105.0, FY2030E 107.1 rising 2%/yr) and far below spot (150.35). FY2025 was a near-normal price year, so 0.405 is a normal-year ratio, not a trough one, and the bull's mean-reversion has no basis.
challenges.answer: Removed the trough framing throughout. FY2025A is a normal benchmark year: the deck's FY2025A marker (108.4) sits marginally above its own long-run level (FY2029E 105.0, lt 105.0), far below spot (150.35), so 0.405 is a normal-year realised-to-benchmark ratio, not a depressed one. The Investment summary, §3 and §5 now say so; the bull's realisation lever is reframed as a mix- driven gain of a couple of points (higher-value offtake narrowing the low-CV discount), not a mean-reversion of a trough ratio, and we no longer call the flat ratio "conservative".

challenges.challenge: qc reports FY2025A ebitda_model 403.56 against ebitda_actual 378.93, a 6.50% gap, with asp_model 43.90 and unit_cost_model 23.60. The report explains the D&A split in prose but never reconciles the EBITDA gap, which is consistent with the historical add-back using only the income-statement depreciation (US$16.5m, F5) while the model's COGS carries the full segment charge (US$37.1m, F16).
challenges.answer: Reconciled the gap in §3 and stated the right side. The pack's FY2025A EBITDA adds back only the income-statement depreciation ({{fact.F5|money}}, F5) while the group's full depreciation and amortisation charge is {{fact.F16|money}} (F16) — the difference is the mine-property depletion carried inside cost of revenue (F20, F21). On the full charge FY2025A EBITDA is about a sixteenth higher than the pack's figure, and the engine's re-priced rebuild lands there (the 6.5% qc gap), agreeing to within a percent. So the pack under-adds the amortisation and is the side that is wrong; the model's side is right, history and forecast are struck on the full charge, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check stays on the reported EBITDA the peer multiples share.

challenges.challenge: The free-float registry flags a step from 10.08% to 12.5% due by 31 March 2027 — a ~2.4pt gap the group can close only by a controller sell-down (the flow that compresses the konglo premium) or by issuing new shares (dilution). The model holds share_change at 0 and the share count flat at 5,882.353m through lt, and neither route is sized as a konglo-regime lever; the report treats the deadline as a pure "overhang" without a quantum.
challenges.answer: Sized the overhang in §6. The gap from the current free float ({{val.konglo.ff.free_float_pct}}, F45) to the first step ({{val.konglo.ff.next_step_pct}} by 31 March 2027) is {{val.konglo.ff.gap_pct}}, about {{val.konglo.ff.months_to_next}} months out, and the group can close it either by a controller sell-down of roughly that share of the capital or by a slightly larger new-share issue (issuing also lifts the denominator). We do not push share_change into the model, because the lens already prices this deadline as a konglo-regime factor — its free-float adjustment — rather than as a fundamental input, and the dated catalyst is in the frontmatter; the report now gives the quantum instead of calling it a bare "overhang".

challenges.challenge: Section 6 presents the related-party channel as a stable "optics-class flag" at 6.94% of cost of revenue (F15). Both related-party channels moved sharply and unexplained: the cost-side ratio fell from 19.13% (FY2024) to 6.94% (FY2025), and related-party sales fell from US$233.1m to US$33.9m (F23), an 85% collapse. A five-fold drop in intra-group purchasing year on year is not a background flag.
challenges.answer: Removed the stable-channel framing. §3 and §6 now state both falls and that the LK does not explain them: related-party cost of revenue fell to {{fact.F15|num2}}% of the total in FY2025 (F15) from roughly a fifth the year before, and related-party revenue fell to {{fact.F23|usdm}} (F23), down more than six-fold, as the buying shifted toward the two third-party contractors above a tenth of revenue (F30). Searched Note 35 (S3, and the FY2024 LK S8) and found no narrative explanation of the swing; we flag it as a governance watch item (optics-class, not manipulation-class) rather than a stable constant.
